- kad-dev-team:acceptance-criteria: Judge and write acceptance criteria that are actually testable — Given/When/Then scenarios, common pitfalls (vague language, specifies-HOW-not-WHAT, happy-path-only, prescriptive UI detail, self-contradiction), and the boundary between AC and Definition of Done. Use whenever acceptance criteria need a quality check, whether or not a new slice is being cut.
- kad-dev-team:accessibility-review: Verify whether a UI-touching slice's rendered artifact — a screen-design mockup today, real built markup once code exists — actually conforms to accessibility standards, rather than merely being designed to make conformance possible. Drives the artifact (keyboard tab-through, computed contrast, DOM structure) rather than only reading its markup. Produces a severity-ranked findings report and turns the result into the slice's accessibility acceptance criteria. Use once a UI-touching slice has a screen-design artifact and its accessibility criteria are still an unfilled placeholder, or whenever a rendered screen needs an accessibility pass.
- kad-dev-team:adr: Write or review an Architecture Decision Record (ADR) once a decision has been made. Use when a decision is architectural, costly to reverse, or non-obvious enough that the reasoning would otherwise be forgotten or re-litigated.
- kad-dev-team:architecture-design: Turn a confirmed, scoped slice into module boundaries and dependency-direction decisions before any code is written — which side owns which interface, what gets isolated behind an adapter, what gets named after which business concept. Use once product-slicer has cut a slice and it's time to decide how it's structured, before implementation starts.
- kad-dev-team:architecture-review: Review existing or changed code against the Dependency Rule, Good Fences, Invasive Species, and Screaming Architecture — catching both premature and missing abstraction, not just import-direction violations. Invoke first, before reading any code, for any request to review a module, directory, PR or codebase for architecture, structure, boundaries, dependencies, layering or design — including a plain "review X for architecture issues" — when a PR touches module boundaries, or before marking architecture-sensitive work as done. Never review architecture without it.
- kad-dev-team:code-review: Review existing or changed code for local, code-level readability — duplication, naming, comments, and function/class-level clarity. Not feature-scope YAGNI (product-slicer's territory) and not structural/architectural abstraction (architecture-review's territory). Use when asked to review code for readability/DRY/naming/comments, or before marking a slice's implementation as done.
- kad-dev-team:design-system: Establish, or on request review and evolve, a project's UI design system — aesthetic direction, design tokens, and core component patterns. Runs once per project as the binding constraint every subsequent screen composes within. Use when a UI-touching slice is about to be designed and no design system exists yet, or when asked to review, audit, or evolve an existing one.
- kad-dev-team:map-query: Answer "does something like this already exist" against the persisted architecture map — a comparable module or interface at the structural level, a comparable function or helper at the implementation level. Read-only; never regenerates the map and never judges whether a returned candidate is close enough to reuse. Use before writing a design doc or before writing code, whenever the question is whether something comparable already exists.
- kad-dev-team:map-update: Regenerate the architecture map from the real codebase — actual import edges, public exports, external packages — and diff it against whatever was recorded before, mechanically flagging duplication candidates and wrong-direction dependency edges. The only skill that writes the map. Use after code changes, once per implementation candidate (throwaway, worktree-scoped) inside a graded build, and once for real after a slice is finalized.
- kad-dev-team:operational-readiness: Check whether something can be shipped safely and recovered when it goes wrong — how you'd know it broke, how you'd put it back, and what someone needs to know when they're debugging it later with no context. Covers rollout strategy, rollback as a tested capability, and the minimum an on-call or future-you needs. Use before shipping a slice, when setting up a delivery path, or when a change is hard to undo.
- kad-dev-team:orchestrator: Route a problem to whichever kad-dev-team persona/skill applies next, by inspecting what already exists (problem doc, scope map, requirements, slices) rather than the user having to name the right persona each time. Use when the user wants to move a problem forward and hasn't said which persona/skill to use, or says "what's next" / "keep going" on a problem already in progress.
- kad-dev-team:pr-writeup: Write a PR description for a completed change that's ready for review. Use when code already exists and needs to be described for a reviewer, distinct from filing not-yet-built work (see user-story-writeup).
- kad-dev-team:problem-framing-doc: Write a one-page problem framing doc — the earliest documentation artifact in a project's life, capturing a real problem before any issue, slice, or code exists. Use when a problem exists but nothing has been scoped yet, and you need something stable for later slicing/architecture work to refer back to.
- kad-dev-team:reliability-requirements: Decide what a slice must do when things go wrong, and what must be observable to know whether it's working — before code exists. Establishes the slice's failure modes, which degrade gracefully versus fail loudly, what target it's held to, and emits testable Given/When/Then criteria. Use when a slice depends on something that can fail, or when "must be reliable" has never been made concrete.
- kad-dev-team:reliability-review: Review existing or changed code and configuration for how it behaves when things go wrong — unhandled failure paths, resilience patterns applied to the wrong failure, resource lifecycle, undiagnosable failure modes, alert quality, and performance problems that are actually correctness problems. Produces a severity-ranked findings report. Invoke first, before reading any code, for any request to review a module, job, PR, route, adapter or alert configuration for production-readiness, reliability, resilience, failure handling, timeouts, retries, observability or alerting — including a plain "is this ready for production?" or "what happens when the database/provider is slow or down?" — and when something works in development but is worrying under real conditions. Never review reliability without it.
- kad-dev-team:requirements-refinement: Pin down the concrete user requirement for one scope-map step (or one small, un-mapped problem) by asking the user directly — who benefits, what they actually want, and why — before any slice gets cut. Use once a step is about to be worked and its WHAT hasn't been confirmed with the user yet, before handing off to product-slicer.
- kad-dev-team:scope-map: Chunk a large problem into a light, named map of steps once a problem framing doc exists but before slicing begins. Use when a problem is big enough that "what's the smallest first slice" doesn't yet answer "what's the whole shape of this" — gives loose visibility into the full problem without designing or slicing any of it.
- kad-dev-team:screen-design: Compose one UI-touching slice's screen within the project's established design system — layout, component composition, and interaction flow. Use once a slice has been cut and a design system already exists (or has just been established) for this project.
- kad-dev-team:security-requirements: Turn a vague security constraint ("must be secure", "handles sensitive data") into concrete, testable acceptance criteria for one slice, before any code exists. Runs a proportional threat pass over the slice, establishes what data and obligations are actually in play by asking, and emits Given/When/Then criteria. Use when a slice carries an unfilled security placeholder, or when a problem doc's security constraint has never been made concrete.
- kad-dev-team:security-review: Review existing or changed code and configuration for reachable security problems — sensitive data escaping through logs/errors/telemetry, injection, missing or bypassed authorization, secrets handling, and over-broad privilege. Produces a severity-ranked findings report. Use when asked to security-review a change, when a PR touches authentication, data handling, or permissions, or before shipping something that handles sensitive data.
- kad-dev-team:staleness-audit: Audit existing documentation for staleness and ceremony. Use when reviewing a docs folder to find entries that mislead, restate the code, exist only for ritual, or disagree with the codebase's actual decision history.
- kad-dev-team:supply-chain-review: Audit a repository's dependency posture against one question — if an upstream package, registry, or maintainer account were compromised right now, would this repo pull the bad version on its next build? Covers packages and lockfiles, CI workflow references, and container base images, plus how accepted findings get recorded. Invoke first, before reading any files, for any request to audit or harden dependencies, lockfiles, pinning, base images or CI action references; to respond to a compromised-package advisory; or to accept, suppress, allowlist, ignore or record a dependency or license finding — including a plain "keep this advisory allowlisted and write it up". Never handle a dependency finding's acceptance without it.
- kad-dev-team:tdd-implementation: Write a designed slice into working code via genuine Red-Green-Refactor, one test at a time from a Test List, or apply a specifically-named fix handed back from any reviewer through that same loop. Use once a slice has an approved design doc and it's time to actually build it, or when a review finding needs a code change.
- kad-dev-team:technology-bootstrap: Decide the smallest set of technology choices that must exist before a slice's first failing test can be written — language, runtime, test runner, package manager and its pinning posture — and explicitly defer everything the slice doesn't force. Recommends with trade-offs and gets approval; never decides unilaterally. Use when a designed slice is about to be implemented in a repo that has no stack yet, or when a later slice forces a technology category nothing has chosen.
- kad-dev-team:test-quality-review: Critique an existing test file's quality — over-mocking, false positives, tests that verify nothing, missing coverage, implementation-detail assertions. Use on demand against any test file, or inline as part of tdd-implementation's own Red-Green-Refactor loop after each cycle.
- kad-dev-team:user-facing-docs: Write user-facing feature documentation for someone other than an engineer. Use when a feature is done and a non-engineer needs to understand why and when to use it.
- kad-dev-team:user-story-writeup: Write up a scoped slice as a trackable work item — a user story describing what's about to be built, before any code exists — or decide whether it should become a filed issue at all and in which system. Use once a slice has been cut (thin path + acceptance criteria) and needs a tracking destination before implementation starts.
- kad-dev-team:vertical-slicing: Cut the smallest end-to-end shippable slice from a problem — picking what to build first, applying slicing techniques when the thinnest path isn't obvious, catching too-big/too-thin scope, and handling scope-creep pushback. Use once a problem framing doc exists and it's time to decide what to build first, or when a proposed slice looks too big, too thin to demo, or scoped by layer instead of by user value.
- kad-dev-team:why-comments: Judge whether a code comment earns its place, using a WHY-not-WHAT test. Use when writing, reviewing, or deciding whether to delete an inline code comment.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's review recipe covers them) at the given effort level (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings up to many, some of them uncertain); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- plugin-authoring: Make a mod: a change to Claude's own interface or behaviour, such as a live pane or panel, a band above the prompt, a status line, a toast, a slash command, or a hook on tool calls or prompts. Use to make, change or debug a mod or its hooks module.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

pattern.description: The glob pattern to match files against

path.description: The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit it for the default behavior. Must be a valid directory path if provided.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
A powerful search tool built on ripgrep

  Usage:
  - ALWAYS use Grep for search tasks. NEVER invoke `grep` or `rg` as a Bash command. The Grep tool has been optimized for correct permissions and access.
  - Supports full regex syntax (e.g., "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+")
  - Filter files with glob parameter (e.g., "*.js", "**/*.tsx") or type parameter (e.g., "js", "py", "rust")
  - Output modes: "content" shows matching lines, "files_with_matches" shows only file paths (default), "count" shows match counts
  - Use Agent tool (if available) for open-ended searches requiring multiple rounds
  - Pattern syntax: Uses ripgrep (not grep) - literal braces need escaping (use `interface\{\}` to find `interface{}` in Go code)
  - Multiline matching: By default patterns match within single lines only. For cross-line patterns like `struct \{[\s\S]*?field`, use `multiline: true`

  Usage:
  - ALWAYS use Grep for search tasks. NEVER invoke `grep` or `rg` as a Bash command. The Grep tool has been optimized for correct permissions and access.

  - Output modes: "content" shows matching lines, "files_with_matches" shows only file paths (default), "count" shows match counts
  - Use Agent tool (if available) for open-ended searches requiring multiple rounds
  - Pattern syntax: Uses ripgrep (not grep) - literal braces need escaping (use `interface\{\}` to find `interface{}` in Go code)

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. - `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms
